title: What if you played basketball on the Moon?
caption:
On the Moon, you'd jump over the hoop. 🏀🌕

Picture a court inside an air-filled dome. The Moon's gravity is 1.62 m/s², about one sixth of Earth's 9.8 m/s².

Same legs, same take-off speed: a 1 m leap on Earth becomes about 6 m up there, feet far above the 3.05 m rim.

And you'd hang in the air for about 5.5 seconds instead of 0.9.

The catch: a normal free throw (about 7.5 m/s) would fly roughly 21 m, about five times too far.

Could you still sink a free throw up there? Yes or no 👇

Send this to the friend who still can't dunk.

Follow @the.impossible.lab for more impossible science.

⚠️ Don't try this. Never jump from heights or hang on a basketball rim: on Earth a fall from a few metres can cause serious injury.

sources: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html (NASA Moon fact sheet: surface gravity 1.62 m/s² vs Earth 9.80 m/s², ratio 0.165 -> ×6.05)
https://www.nbcsports.com/nba/news/keon-johnson-sets-nba-draft-combine-record-with-48-inch-vertical-leap (NBA combine record max vertical 48 in = 1.22 m; an elite leap of ~1 m is conservative)
https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1702.07234 (free-throw physics: release height ~2 m, distance ~4.6 m, measured release speeds 7.0–7.8 m/s at ~47–57°)
NBA court dimensions: rim 10 ft = 3.05 m, rim centre 5 ft 3 in from the baseline, free-throw line 15 ft from the backboard, court 94 × 50 ft
Computed: take-off speed of a 1.0 m Earth leap v = √(2·9.80·1.0) = 4.43 m/s; on the Moon h = v²/(2·1.62) = 6.05 m, airtime 2v/g = 5.47 s (Earth 0.90 s)

Computed (numerical, air drag Cd 0.47, ball r 0.12 m, m 0.6 kg, ρ 1.2 kg/m³ inside the dome): a free throw at 7.55 m/s, 52°, that reaches the rim 4.2 m away on Earth travels ≈21 m before dropping back to rim height on the Moon (×5.1); ≈33 m without air
